column4: After the earth expels its burdens in 99:2 and reports its news in 99:4, this ayah says people come out in separate groups to see their deeds; it is the immediate human counterpart to the section's opening of graves and disclosure of what was inside.

After 27:74 says the Lord knows what breasts conceal and declare, this ayah adds that nothing hidden in heaven or earth escapes the clear record, completing the section's link between inward contents and the final account.

This ayah says God will resurrect people, inform them of their deeds, and that He counted what they forgot; it directly matches the section's account that remains complete even when its contents are no longer remembered.

The section cites the particle's weight as the scale's fineness; this ayah says not even an atom's weight or anything smaller or larger escapes the Lord's knowledge and clear record, a repeated formulation of exact accounting.
In another formulation, this ayah says nothing as small as an atom's weight in heaven or earth is hidden from God or absent from the clear record, extending the section's particle-sized reckoning.
The section's sorting reaches even the smallest measure; this ayah says God does not wrong an atom's weight and multiplies a good deed, pairing exact measure with a just distinction of outcomes.

The section describes the final account exposing what was inside; this ayah says each soul will find its good and evil deeds present and wish the evil far away, a concrete disclosure of both sides of the account.
The section pictures the shell being removed so what is inside can be seen; this ayah says the person's covering is removed and sight becomes sharp, a precise end-time parallel to unveiling.
This ayah says the earth is laid bare, everyone is gathered with no one left behind, continuing the section's image of the buried being brought out into a complete reckoning.
After none are left out of the gathering in 18:47, this ayah says all stand before their Lord and are brought as at first creation, completing the exposure and accounting scene.

The section describes extraction as labor carried through to a final result; this ayah addresses the person as striving toward the Lord and meeting Him, giving that work-and-arrival structure an explicit parallel.
The section contrasts inward truth with outward appearance; this ayah contrasts people who greet believers warmly with the rage they show in private and says God knows what breasts contain.

In the Uhud passage that leads to the section's 3:154 example, this ayah distinguishes those who wanted this world from those who wanted the Hereafter, making battle behavior expose the attachment within.
This ayah joins attractive public speech to what is in the heart, which is hostile; it directly meets the section's contrast between the chest's hidden contents and outward appearance.

The section treats the chest as a vessel that accumulates what a person takes in; this ayah says deeds have left a rust upon hearts, a specific image of the inward store being marked by accumulated action.

This ayah contrasts saying “we believe” with faith not yet entering the heart, a direct case of outward claim and inward condition differing as the section's appearance/interior distinction describes.
The section links what is buried to what will be brought out for judgment; this ayah places the buried-alive girl before that judgment, turning a concealed burial into an exposed case.
After the buried girl is brought into view in 81:8, this ayah asks what crime she was killed for, making the disclosure a reckoning of what had been hidden.
This ayah says mouths are sealed while hands and feet testify to what people did, a specific way concealed deeds become visible at judgment.
This ayah likewise has tongues, hands, and feet testify to what people did; it repeats the bodily disclosure scene in another judgment passage.
The section sets intense love of wealth beside its grain/kernel wordplay; this ayah names rivalry in piling up more, a concrete enactment of that attachment.
This ayah says the piling up continues until people visit the graves, directly meeting the section's two images of wealth attachment and graves opened at resurrection.
The section says the final account reveals what was produced by labor; this ayah says a person's effort will be seen, a direct parallel to the deed becoming visible.
After 53:40 says effort will be seen, this ayah says it will then be repaid in full, completing the section's image of a final account.
After the earth casts out what is within in 84:4, this ayah says it listens to its Lord and is bound to do so, giving the disclosure scene its commanded cause.

Following the person whose words and heart diverge in 2:204, this ayah shows him corrupting the land and destroying crops and offspring, joining the hidden heart to a concrete agricultural consequence.

This ayah depicts a man hiding from people in shame and debating whether to keep a daughter in disgrace or bury her in the ground; it gives a concrete, contrary instance of an inward state hidden as burial.
This ayah answers the denial of resurrection by saying God can gather a person's bones, a specific bodily gathering parallel to the section's opened graves.
After promising to gather the bones in 75:3, this ayah says God can even proportion the fingertips, extending the resurrection image to minute detail.
This ayah says every soul is held in pledge for what it earned, a direct account of the deeds collected within and brought to judgment.
Before the effort is seen and repaid in 53:40–41, this ayah says a person has only what they strove for, specifying what enters that final account.

In the same passage as the section's gathering-and-hoarding parallel at 70:18, this ayah says that when good reaches a person, he withholds it, specifying the possessive impulse behind intense love of wealth.

Following 3:141's purification of believers after Uhud, this ayah asks whether people think they will enter the Garden before the strivers and patient are made known, extending the section's trial-and-purification image.
This ayah repeats that abiding good deeds are better in reward and return, a direct parallel to the section's dictionary sense of what remains after other things pass.
